Flow control lets one endpoint tell the other to stop transmitting. It is needed because the two nodes often have different capacities: communication adjusts to that of the weaker one.

The simplest way is stop and wait: I send a message and do not send another until I receive its acknowledgment. If the receiver cannot store more, it does not acknowledge.

With A and B far apart and a round trip delay of 250 ms, one message goes out every 250 ms: barely 4 packets per second.
Stop and wait slows the sender well, but wastes the link: almost all the time is spent waiting.

The sliding window improves the scheme: several packets are sent without waiting for acknowledgment. With a window of 4, A sends four in a row and cannot send the fifth until it receives the ACK of the first. Each acknowledgment frees room for one more packet.

The window size depends on the devices' capacity, on the bandwidth, and on the end-to-end delay: at twice the distance (500 ms), the same window yields only 8 packets per second.
This is how HDLC works: the window is measured in messages and each ACK, besides acknowledging, allows sending the next one.
TCP separates acknowledging from granting permission

In HDLC, acknowledging and granting permission are the same thing. If B received a frame correctly but wants no more, it has to hold back the ACK, leaving unacknowledged something that did arrive: flow control interferes with error control.

TCP separates them with a credit scheme. Each acknowledgment carries two pieces of data:

  • ACK = i: I received everything up to i − 1; I expect i.
  • Window = j: you may send me j octets, from i to i + j − 1.
The credit is the buffer that the receiver's operating system reserved for the connection. It is measured in bytes, not messages, and each endpoint grants its own to the other.
Example: ACK = 30, Window = 64240 → I received up to octet 29 and you may send me from 30 to 64269. An endpoint can acknowledge data without allowing more.

Stallings' example, with 200-byte segments. B had granted A a credit of 1400 octets starting at 1001: A can send from 1001 to 2400, and B keeps that count too.

The application hands A three blocks. TCP encapsulates them with sequence numbers 1001, 1201, and 1401 (that of the first byte of each).

With each transmission A shrinks its window: it consumed 600 and has 800 left.
The sender deducts credit when sending, without waiting for the segment to arrive or to be acknowledged.
Stallings: B acknowledges and grants less credit

B receives the three segments and acknowledges them with ACK = 1601. But it does not return all the credit: it can only receive 200 bytes beyond the original window, so it announces Window = 1000 (from 1601 to 2600).

While that acknowledgment is in transit, the application gives A two more blocks: they go out with sequence 1601 and 1801.

A has sent five segments without receiving anything: it used 1000 of the 1400 and has 400 left.
To the 800 A had left, B adds 200. But A only learns of it when the acknowledgment arrives; meanwhile it works with what it has.
Stallings: the credit arrives… and the brake

A receives ACK = 1601, Window = 1000. Its window now runs from 1601 to 2600, and it has already used 400 with the last two segments (still in transit): 600 left. B, on receiving them, does the same math.

If B runs out of room or cannot keep up processing, it can stop A without ceasing to acknowledge: ACK = 2001, Window = 0. It received everything up to 2000 correctly, but the credit is zero.
Whatever A sent above 2000 before finding out is considered lost: B has nowhere to put it, and it will have to be resent when B grants credit again.
The window as seen from the sender

For the sender, the byte sequence is split into three zones:

  • Acknowledged data: sent and with the ACK received.
  • Data sent but unacknowledged: from the number of the last ACK received up to the next sequence number to send.
  • Transmission allowed: from the next sequence number up to the end of the window (the credit).

That is why it is "sliding": the back edge advances with each ACK and the front edge with each credit.

The Window field is 16 bits wide: at most 65535 bytes. The window scale factor option was born for very high delay links, such as a geostationary satellite (round trip delay on the order of 500 ms): many packets must be in transit while the ACKs take a long time to come back.

Today the same happens with high bandwidth links: what counts is the relationship between bandwidth and delay.

The option carries a value, for example 8, and the Window field is multiplied by 2⁸ = 256.
In the capture, Window = 513 with factor 256: the real window is 513 × 256 = 131328 bytes, impossible to write in 16 bits.

Retransmission: how long to wait for the ACK

TCP only has positive acknowledgment: there is no rejection. If the ACK of a segment does not arrive within the RTO (Retransmission Time Out), it is retransmitted.

The RTO is specific to each connection: within Buenos Aires the round trip delay is around 10 ms; to Europe, around 250 ms.

  • Too short: something that had arrived correctly is resent; extra traffic and duplicate copies.
  • Too long (400 ms for an RTD of 10): on a loss, the sender sits idle waiting.
The RTO must be a function of the round trip delay: a bit more, never less and not much more. The Timestamp option allows measuring it precisely to adjust the RTO.
Flow and errors, each with its own field

• Flow control: lets the receiver slow the sender.
  • Stop and wait → sliding window → byte credits.
  • ACK = i, Window = j: I received up to i − 1; you may send from i to i + j − 1.
  • Window = 0 stops the sender without ceasing to acknowledge.
  • Window scale: windows larger than 65535 bytes.
  • Positive ACK only; with no ACK within the RTO, it retransmits.

The credit says how much the other endpoint can receive, not how much the network in between can take. Congestion control handles that, in the next lesson.
Sequence + ACK → what arrived (error control) · Window → how much more can be sent (flow control) · Options → Window scale and Timestamp.
With stop and wait and a 250 ms round trip delay, how many packets are sent per second?
Each packet takes 125 ms to arrive and its ACK another 125 ms to return: one every 250 ms, that is, 4 per second.
A receives a segment with ACK = 1601 and Window = 1000. Up to which byte is it allowed to send?
The credit runs from i to i + j − 1: from 1601 to 1601 + 1000 − 1 = 2600.
